title: Question 8
stem:
Fig. 8.1 shows the three lowest-frequency lines in the part of the emission spectrum for hydrogen that relates to electron transitions to the ground state (level $n = 1$).

{{figure:figure_8_1}}

Fig. 8.1 (not to scale)

The numbers represent the frequencies, in $10^{15}\text{Hz}$, associated with the spectral lines.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Use the photon model of electromagnetic radiation to explain how the existence of spectral lines in the emission spectrum provides evidence for discrete electron energy levels in the hydrogen atom.

markscheme_points.text: Any three points from: electrons moving between levels emit a single photon; energy of photon = difference between energy levels; energy of photon depends on frequency; discrete frequencies (in spectrum) so differences between electron energies must be discrete; discrete differences between electron energies means energy levels must be discrete

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is happening inside the atom when light is emitted - where does the electron start and finish?
Hint 2: Remember how the energy carried away by one packet of light is linked to the colour or frequency of that line.
Hint 3: Link the observation that only certain separate frequencies appear to what that must mean for the allowed electron energies.
parts.proper_answer: An electron falling to a lower level emits a single photon with energy equal to the difference in level energies, $E = hf$. Only discrete frequencies $f$ are observed, so $\Delta E$ values are discrete, hence the electron energy levels themselves must be discrete.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What emission means**
Think of an electron high up in the atom falling down toward the ground state $n=1$. It cannot lose energy gradually. It makes one jump and gives all the lost energy to one single photon that flies out.

Step 2: **Photon energy fixes the colour**
For that photon, $$E_{photon} = hf = E_{upper} - E_{lower}$$ So each possible jump gives one exact frequency $f$. A continuous range of energies would give a continuous rainbow, not thin lines.

Step 3: **Discrete lines means discrete levels**
Fig. 8.1 shows only separate sharp lines at $2.47$, $2.92$, $3.09 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$. Discrete $f$ means discrete $hf$, so discrete differences $\Delta E$. That is only possible if the electron energies themselves can only have certain separate values.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: The energy of the ground state (level $n = 1$) in a hydrogen atom is $-13.6\text{eV}$.
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in $\text{J}$, of the ground state.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what $1\text{ eV}$ means in joules - the energy gained by one electron charge $e$ moved through $1\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert eV to J**
$1\text{ eV}$ is the energy of charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ through $1\text{ V}$, so $$1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$$ Multiply, keeping the negative sign which shows the electron is bound: $$E = -13.6 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}$$

hints: Hint 1: Recall what $1\text{ eV}$ means in joules - the energy gained by one electron charge $e$ moved through $1\text{ V}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the energy difference between levels $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ is $10.2\text{eV}$.
hints: Hint 1: Identify which line in Fig. 8.1 corresponds to the smallest jump to $n=1$, that is from $n=2$, and note its frequency including the $10^{15}$ factor.
Hint 2: Plan to calculate the photon energy in joules first, then divide by the electron charge to express it in eV to show the required value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick the correct frequency**
The lowest frequency line is the smallest energy jump to the ground state, so $n=2$ to $n=1$. From Fig. 8.1, $$f = 2.47 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$$

Step 2: **Apply $\Delta E = hf$ and convert to eV**
Photon energy equals the level difference: $$\Delta E = hf$$ $$\Delta E = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 2.47 \times 10^{15} = 1.64 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}$$ Divide by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ to get eV: $$\Delta E = \frac{1.64 \times 10^{-18}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 10.2\text{ eV}$$ This is the $n=2$ to $n=1$ separation.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
Complete Table 8.1 to show the energy differences from the ground state, and the energies of the levels up to $n = 4$, in the hydrogen atom. Use the space for any working.

Table 8.1

| level | (energy difference from $n = 1$)/$\text{eV}$ | energy/$\text{eV}$ |
| $n = 4$ |  |  |
| $n = 3$ |  |  |
| $n = 2$ | 10.2 |  |
| $n = 1$ | 0.0 | $-13.6$ |

markscheme_points.text: n = 3 energy level = - 1.5 eV and n = 4 energy level = - 0.8 eV

hints: Hint 1: Match each remaining frequency to its starting level - larger frequency means larger jump to $n=1$, so $2.92$ is from $n=3$ and $3.09$ is from $n=4$.
Hint 2: Use the same $E = hf$ method as in (b)(ii) to find each energy difference in joules, then convert to eV.
Hint 3: Remember the level energy is found by adding the difference to the ground state: $E_n = -13.6\text{ eV} + \Delta E$.
Hint 4: Check your table makes sense - higher $n$ means less negative energy, closer to zero, and differences should be about $12.1\text{ eV}$ and $12.8\text{ eV}$.
parts.proper_answer: energy difference $n=2$: $10.2\text{ eV}$, energy $n=2$: $-3.4\text{ eV}$; difference $n=3$: $12.1\text{ eV}$, energy $n=3$: $-1.5\text{ eV}$; difference $n=4$: $12.8\text{ eV}$, energy $n=4$: $-0.85\text{ eV}$ approx $-0.8\text{ eV}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the $n=2$ level energy**
You already know $\Delta E_{2-1} = 10.2\text{ eV}$. Add to ground state: $$E_2 = -13.6 + 10.2 = -3.4\text{ eV}$$

Step 2: **Calculate the $n=3$ difference**
Use $f = 2.92 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$: $$\Delta E_3 = hf = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 2.92 \times 10^{15} = 1.94 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}$$ $$\Delta E_3 = \frac{1.94 \times 10^{-18}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 12.1\text{ eV}$$ Then $$E_3 = -13.6 + 12.1 = -1.5\text{ eV}$$

Step 3: **Calculate the $n=4$ difference**
Use $f = 3.09 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$: $$\Delta E_4 = hf = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.09 \times 10^{15} = 2.05 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}$$ $$\Delta E_4 = \frac{2.05 \times 10^{-18}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 12.8\text{ eV}$$ Then $$E_4 = -13.6 + 12.8 = -0.8\text{ eV}$$

Step 4: **Complete Table 8.1**
Higher $n$ is less tightly bound, so energy is less negative. Table: $n=2$: $10.2$, $-3.4$; $n=3$: $12.1$, $-1.5$; $n=4$: $12.8$, $-0.8$, all in eV.
